entry.title: Application by Birrang Enterprise Development Co Ltd [2026] FWC 4167
entry.content:
The Fair Work Commission considered Birrang’s application under s 120 of the Fair Work Act 2009 to reduce Mr Reid’s redundancy pay because it had offered him redeployment into a Support Coordinator role. Mr Reid declined the role but consented to the application. The Commission reduced his redundancy entitlement from four weeks to three weeks’ pay.

Key holding: Under s 120(1)(b)(i), whether alternative employment is acceptable is assessed objectively by the Commission, not by the employee’s subjective view, and if the preconditions are met the Commission has a broad discretion under s 120(2) to reduce redundancy pay.

Whether the alternative employment is "acceptable" is to be determined objectively, not by reference to whether Mr Reid considered that it was subjectively acceptable. The determination of whether alternative employment is acceptable requires me to make an assessment and value judgment.

entry.title: Ms Diane Hamilton v EDMI Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 4187
entry.content:
Ms Hamilton lodged a general protections dismissal application alleging adverse action based on workplace rights, disability, and temporary absence. She filed 82 days out of time and sought an extension under s 366(1) of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth). The Fair Work Commission refused the extension and dismissed the application.

Key holding: Stress or illness associated with a dismissal does not by itself establish exceptional circumstances for an extension of time; the applicant must show the condition caused or explained the delay.

The stress that accompanies a dismissal will not, without more, favour a finding of exceptional circumstances.

entry.title: Estefania Asensio Tato v Lycée Condorcet Trading AS The International French School Of Sydney Ltd [2026] FWC 4154
entry.content:
The Fair Work Commission dealt with a s 739 dispute brought by a former secondary Spanish teacher against her former school over alleged underpayments/classification for February and March 2025 work. The Commission upheld the school’s jurisdictional objection because the dispute was not raised until after employment ended, dismissed the application, and noted any underpayment claim could be pursued in court. The deed of release was not determinative.

Key holding: Under s 739 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth), the Commission lacks jurisdiction to determine an enterprise agreement dispute where the dispute is raised after the employment relationship has ended.

The entitlements conferred in the Agreement remain enforceable for a limited period on application to the relevant Court, but the Commission is unable to deal with the dispute under the dispute resolution clause where the dispute was raised after the employment relationship had ended.

entry.title: Ms Joy Bultman v The Trustee For Scrappy's Metal Recycling Trust [2026] FWC 4149
entry.content:
Ms Joy Bultman applied under s.394 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) for an unfair dismissal remedy against The Trustee For Scrappy’s Metal Recycling Trust. She failed to attend a Commission mention/conference, did not comply with directions, filed no material by the deadline, and gave no explanation. Deputy President Bell dismissed the application for want of prosecution and no reasonable prospects of success in Bultman v The Trustee For Scrappy’s Metal Recycling Trust [2026] FWC 4149.

Key holding: Under s.587(1) of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth), the Commission may dismiss an application for failure to prosecute, including non-compliance with directions or failure to attend, and where no evidence means no reasonable prospects of success.

I am satisfied the power to dismiss can extend to circumstances where an applicant has failed to prosecute his or her case, including by non -compliance with directions to attend a mention/conference or file material and a repeated failure to provide a proper explanation for that non -compliance.

entry.title: Application by dnata Airport Services Pty Ltd Trading AS dnata [2026] FWC 4178
entry.content:
The Fair Work Commission considered whether to approve dnata’s Queensland passenger services enterprise agreement [2026] FWC 4178. The TWU opposed approval, arguing the Agreement did not pass the better off overall test (BOOT), particularly regarding part-time shiftworker overtime and pay rates that might fall below the Award. The Commission largely accepted dnata’s Award construction and BOOT approach, but required further information or an undertaking about part-time day workers before approval.

Key holding: The BOOT is assessed at the test time, and the Commission does not speculate about future unknown Award wage outcomes when deciding whether employees are better off overall.

I accept the Applicant 's submission to the effect that it is not for the Commission to speculate about potential future unknown wage outcomes in assessing the BOOT, and that the BOOT is to be applied at test time.

entry.title: Ms Karen McClear v A Team Tuition Australia Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 4174
entry.content:
Ms McClear resigned after a lengthy suspension pending an unresolved misconduct investigation and brought a s 365 general protections claim alleging she was forced to resign. A Team Tuition objected that she was not dismissed within s 386. The Commission dismissed the application, finding she was not forced to resign because of the employer’s conduct and was therefore not dismissed.

Key holding: A resignation is a dismissal under s 386(1)(b) only where an objective assessment of the employer’s conduct shows it made resignation the probable result or left the employee with no effective or real choice but to resign.

In making that assessment, it is appropriate to make an objective analysis of the Respondent's conduct to determine whether it was of such a nature that resignation was the probable result or that the employee had no effective or real choice but to resign.

entry.title: Ms Mariama Serray Turay v Pegasus Community Care Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 4186
entry.content:
The Fair Work Commission dealt with Ms Turay’s unfair dismissal application, which was filed before the dismissal ultimately relied on took effect. The Commission found her employment was terminated on 16 September 2026 after an earlier 30 June 2026 termination notice was withdrawn by consent, so the 7 September 2026 application was premature. The Commission declined to waive the irregularity and dismissed the application.

Key holding: The Commission may decline to waive the irregularity in a premature unfair dismissal application where the applicant had a clear opportunity to withdraw and file a new application within time but did not do so.

As to whether Ms Turay could have discontinued the Application and filed a new application within time, this factor weights against waiving the irregularity.

entry.title: "Automotive, Food, Metals, Engineering, Printing and Kindred Industries Union" known as the Australian Manufacturing Workers' Union (AMWU) (188V) v Applus Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 4190
entry.content:
The AMWU applied under s 739 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) for the Fair Work Commission to resolve a dispute over clause 17.2 of the Applus Pty Ltd Onshore NDT & Inspection Greenfields Agreement 2025. The issue was whether Easter Saturday and Easter Sunday, both falling on a weekend, entitled employees to public holidays on the next two working days or only the next working day. The Commission held each public holiday had to be taken on successive next working days.

Key holding: Under clause 17.2, where two gazetted public holidays fall on a weekend, each holiday must be taken on successive next working days so employees receive both entitlements.

Having considered the text, context and purpose, I find that the answer to the question is that employees were entitled to take the Easter Saturday public holiday on Tuesday, 7 April 2026, and the Easter Sunday public holiday on Wednesday, 8 April 2026.

entry.title: "Automotive, Food, Metals, Engineering, Printing and Kindred Industries Union" known as the Australian Manufacturing Workers' Union (AMWU) (188V) v Schindler Lifts Australia Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 4166
entry.content:
The AMWU referred a dispute under s.739 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) and clause 10 of the Schindler Lifts Australia Pty Ltd Victorian Enterprise Agreement 2024–2028, asking how the "make up pay for workers comp" entitlement in clause 42 is calculated. The Commission held that "average weekly earnings" in clause 42 is to be worked out by reference to the Victorian workers' compensation concept of pre-injury average weekly earnings under the WIRC Act, and left the arithmetic to the parties.

Key holding: Where an enterprise agreement requires a top-up to 100% of "average weekly earnings" but does not define the term, that expression is to be calculated by reference to the pre-injury average weekly earnings concept in the Victorian workers' compensation legislation, with either s.153(1) or s.153(2) of the WIRC Act available.

As such, I consider that Mr Savari's 'average weekly earnings' for the purposes of clause 42 of the 2024 Agreement in relation to his workers' compensation claim for injury for the injury on 20 March 2025 are able to be calculated by reference to either s.153(1) or s.153(2) of the WIRC Act.

The application was dismissed.

entry.title: Elizabeth O'Donnell v Fresleven Pty Ltd ATF The Muley Graves Unit Trust T/As Coral Bay Ecotours & Roger Bailye and Others [2026] FWC 4171
entry.content:
Ms O’Donnell brought a s.365 general protections application against Fresleven Pty Ltd and others, alleging she had been dismissed. The Commission determined a jurisdictional objection that she had not been dismissed. Deputy President O’Keeffe found no dismissal was communicated, upheld the objection and dismissed the application.

Key holding: A termination of employment is not effective unless the employer communicates it to the employee in clear and unequivocal terms; allusion or insinuation is insufficient.

As I read them the proposition is that an employee is not terminated until they are advised in clear and unequivocal terms that they are terminated. It is not sufficient to allude or insinuate - the employee must be told.

entry.title: Application by Queensland Police Citizens Youth Welfare Association [2026] FWC 4157
entry.content:
The Fair Work Commission determined an employer’s application under s.120 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) to reduce Ms Ashleigh Silver’s redundancy pay to nil after it offered her redeployment to another OSHC Educator role. entry.title: Application by Raquel Gray [2026] FWC 4143
entry.content:
The Fair Work Commission determined an unfair termination remedy application by a regulated road transport contractor, Ms Gray, against BESB Couriers after she was replaced on the Toukley delivery run upon returning from leave. The Commission found there was no valid reason for termination and that the Road Transport Industry Termination Code processes were not followed, so the termination was unfair. It ordered that a new services contract be entered into between BESB Couriers and Ms Gray personally.

Key holding: A regulated road transport contractor’s termination is unfair where there is no valid reason for termination and the processes under the Road Transport Industry Termination Code are not followed.

In summary, there was no valid reason for the termination of the services contract, and the processes in the Road Transport Code were not followed, in part because of a breakdown in communication and in part because BESB Couriers is a small business with l imited access to resources or relevant legal or human resources expertise. I am satisfied that the termination of the services contract was unfair.

entry.title: Mr Peter Deane v Hawkesbury Pools Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 4093
entry.content:
The Fair Work Commission dismissed Mr Deane’s unfair dismissal application against Hawkesbury Pools Pty Ltd ([2026] FWC 4093). The employer established it was a small business and that the summary dismissal for establishing and advertising a competing business was consistent with the Small Business Fair Dismissal Code. Because Code consistency meant the dismissal could not be unfair, the Commission did not determine the merits.

Key holding: For a summary dismissal under the Small Business Fair Dismissal Code, the Commission determines whether the employer held a belief that the employee’s conduct was sufficiently serious to justify immediate dismissal and whether that belief was based on reasonable grounds, not whether the dismissal was valid or warranted.

First, there needs to be a consideration whether, at the time of dismissal, the employer held a belief that the employee's conduct was sufficiently serious to justify immediate dismissal. Secondly it is necessary to consider whether that belief was based on reasonable grounds.

entry.title: Rasier Pacific Pty Ltd v Ali Hamza [2026] FWC 4164
entry.content:
Uber sought a stay under s 606 of the Fair Work Act 2009 of a Fair Work Commission order requiring it to reactivate Mr Ali Hamza’s access to its digital platform pending appeal. At first instance the Commissioner found moderate speeding was not a valid reason for deactivation and that Uber had not complied with the Digital Labour Platform Deactivation Code. Deputy President Easton refused the stay, finding no reasonable prospects on the merits and no balance of convenience favouring it.

Key holding: A stay under s 606 requires an arguable case with reasonable prospects on both permission to appeal and the substantive merits, together with a balance of convenience favouring the stay.

In determining whether to grant a stay application the Commission must be satisfied that there is an arguable case, with some reasonable prospect of success, in respect of both the question of leave to appeal and the substantive merits of the appeal. In addition, the balance of convenience must weigh in favour of the order subject to appeal being stayed.

entry.title: Daniel Cowell v Brief Access Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 4165
entry.content:
The Fair Work Commission dealt with an unfair dismissal application by Daniel Cowell against Brief Access Pty Ltd (the named respondent; the extract also refers to Brief Labour Co Pty Ltd). The Commission rejected the employer’s jurisdictional objection that it was a small business entitled to rely on the Small Business Fair Dismissal Code, found the dismissal unfair, declined reinstatement and ordered compensation. The extract does not reproduce the final compensation calculation or full orders.

Key holding: To rely on summary dismissal under the Small Business Fair Dismissal Code, an employer’s belief that conduct is sufficiently serious must be based on reasonable grounds, ordinarily including discussion with the employee and regard to their explanation.

Normally in order to hold a belief on reasonable grounds it will be necessary to have a discussion with the employee about the perceived serious misconduct and pay regard to the explanations and views given by the employee.

entry.title: Jason Perry v Australian Port Service (Qld) Pty Ltd Trading AS Ausport Marine [2026] FWC 4146

entry.title: Doran Herrick v Bupa Aged Care Australia Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 4141
entry.content:
In [2026] FWC 4141, Mr Herrick lodged an unfair dismissal application after his May 2025 dismissal from Bupa Aged Care Australia Pty Ltd, despite having signed an Employee Separation Agreement containing release and bar-to-proceedings clauses. The Fair Work Commission found the agreement constituted a binding settlement, declined a stay, and dismissed the application under s 587(1)(c).

Key holding: A binding settlement or accord and satisfaction extinguishes the existing cause of action and replaces it with a new cause based on the agreement, so an unfair dismissal application barred by an executed separation agreement has no reasonable prospects of success.

In Australian Postal Corporation v Gorman1, Besanko J held that the existence of a binding settlement or 'accord and satisfaction' extinguishes the existing cause of action and replaces it with a new cause of action based on the agreement. That is the case in the matter before me.

entry.title: Charles Patterson v P.A.P. Heating Solutions Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 4135
entry.content:
The Fair Work Commission considered an unfair dismissal application by Mr Patterson against a small business employer, PAP Heating. The dismissal was for alleged performance issues, but the employer’s written warning did not state that dismissal was at risk and the employer terminated before a promised meeting. The Commission found the dismissal unfair and awarded compensation.

Key holding: To satisfy the “Other dismissal” limb of the Small Business Fair Dismissal Code, a small business employer must expressly warn the employee that dismissal is at risk if performance does not improve, not merely that further action may follow.

However, the warning did not say that Mr Pa tterson was at risk of being dismissed if there was no improvement. As a result, the dismissal was not consistent with the Small Business Code.

The AMWU and CEPU are noted as covered, and the Manufacturing Award delegates’ rights clause is taken to be a term because the agreement lacked a compliant term.

Key holding: Where an enterprise agreement does not contain a delegates’ rights term meeting s.205A, the relevant award delegates’ rights clause is taken to be a term of the agreement under s.205A(2).

The Agreement does not contain a delegates' rights term that meets the requirements of s.205A of the FW Act. Accordingly, pursuant to s.205A(2) of the FW Act, clause 40A of the Manufacturing and Associated Industries and Occupations Award 2020 is taken to be a term of the Agreement.
